question: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle?
title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) explained
direct_answer: The Liskov Substitution Principle says code written for a base type should continue to meet its contract when given any subtype. The subtype must accept the base type's valid uses, preserve required results and invariants, and avoid removing promised capabilities. Compiling under the same type is not enough.

sections.title: Understanding Behavioral Substitution
sections.content:
The **Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)** is a behavioral rule for subtyping. If a function works with a base type, supplying a subtype should not invalidate the guarantees that function relies on.

A subtype should not require stronger inputs than the base contract, return weaker results, break invariants, or remove guaranteed operations. It may provide a more specific result or stronger guarantee when clients can still use it through the base type.

The familiar mutable rectangle/square example depends on the base contract allowing width and height to change independently. A square cannot preserve that setter behavior. Immutable shapes with an `area()` contract do not have the same conflict. LSP is about the declared and observable contract, not the names of the classes.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Substitutability|~LSP core|subtype usable wherever base is|no surprises for callers
blue|Classic Break|~Square / Rectangle|setWidth changes height|the area assertion fails
emerald|Rules|~honor the contract|don't strengthen preconditions|don't weaken postconditions
violet|Symptom|~runtime surprise|child throws or no-ops where base works

sections.title: Classic Rectangle-Square LSP Violation
When LSP Matters Most
sections.content: Apply LSP thinking when designing service hierarchies in Spring Boot. If you have a **PaymentProcessor** interface with implementations like StripePaymentProcessor and PayPalPaymentProcessor, any code using PaymentProcessor must work identically with both — same error handling, same transaction guarantees, same idempotency behavior. LSP is critical in framework code: if you extend Spring's AbstractController and override methods, framework code calling those methods must still work. It's also vital in **repository patterns** — if you have CachedUserRepository extending DatabaseUserRepository, operations like save() and findById() must behave consistently, not skip the database or return stale data.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inheritance based on real-world taxonomy**: Freshers see "Square is a Rectangle in math" and create that inheritance, ignoring that the behavioral contract (independent width/height) doesn't match.
- **Thinking compilation equals correctness**: If your Square subclass compiles when passed to a method expecting Rectangle, freshers assume LSP is satisfied — but runtime assertion failures or wrong calculations reveal the violation.
- **Overriding with narrower behavior**: Creating a ReadOnlyUserRepository that extends UserRepository but throws exceptions on save() — callers expecting UserRepository get runtime crashes. The compiler allows it, but it violates the substitution principle.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: A subtype must preserve the observable contract of its base type.
Valid base inputs must remain valid; required results and invariants must remain true.
A subtype must not remove capabilities the base contract guarantees.
Type compatibility at compile time is not enough.
Judge the actual contract, not only a real-world is-a label.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The Liskov Substitution Principle says that code written against a base type should remain correct when any subtype is supplied. The compiler checks method signatures; LSP checks the behavior that clients are promised.

For example, if a mutable `Rectangle` contract lets a caller set width and height independently, a `Square` subtype cannot preserve that contract because changing one side changes the other. If both are immutable `Shape` implementations exposing only `area()`, the conflict disappears because the contract is different.

A safe subtype does not strengthen preconditions, weaken required results, break invariants, or remove guaranteed operations. The design question is whether the replacement preserves client-observable behavior, not whether the subtype has a mathematically related name.

question: How do you fix a Liskov Substitution Principle violation?
title: Fixing LSP violations — composition vs inheritance
direct_answer: Fix an LSP violation by first identifying the broken base guarantee. You may correct the subtype, narrow or redesign the base contract, split capabilities into interfaces, or replace inheritance with composition. Removing inheritance is common, but it is not the only fix; the result must make every advertised subtype honor the contract.

sections.title: Fixing LSP Violations Through Design
sections.content:
Start by writing the **base guarantee** that the subtype breaks. Does it reject a valid input, return a weaker result, change an invariant, or remove an operation? The repair depends on that mismatch.

Sometimes the subtype is simply wrong and can be corrected. Sometimes the base type promises too much, so its contract should be narrowed or split into capability interfaces. When the relationship is not truly substitutable, independent implementations or composition are clearer than inheritance.

For mutable square and rectangle types, a common repair is an immutable `Shape` contract with separate implementations, or separate dimension-changing capabilities. For a cached service, composition can wrap a correct service while preserving all result and failure guarantees. Tests should run the same contract cases against every implementation.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Spot It|~broken contract|subclass throws or no-ops|behaves unlike the base
blue|Fix 1|~rethink hierarchy|extract a common base|Square and Rectangle → Shape
emerald|Fix 2|~composition|hold the behavior, don't inherit it
violet|Fix 3|~segregate|capability interfaces (ties to ISP)

sections.title: Fixing Rectangle-Square with Interface
When to Apply Each Fix
sections.content:
Use the **interface approach** when subclasses have fundamentally different state or invariants — Rectangle has two independent dimensions, Square has one constrained dimension, so shared setters make no sense.

Use **composition** when you want to reuse some parent behavior but need to override or skip parts — a CachingUserService can compose a DatabaseUserService and call it only on cache misses.

Use **strategy pattern** when behavior varies at runtime — instead of inheritance for different payment types, inject a PaymentStrategy. In Spring Boot, favor **dependency injection of interfaces** over extending concrete service classes. If you find yourself adding throws UnsupportedOperationException to overridden methods, that's a signal you need one of these fixes, not inheritance.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Throwing UnsupportedOperationException**: Freshers think overriding a method to throw this exception is a valid fix — it's actually another LSP violation because callers still break at runtime.
- **Abstract parent class with no-op methods**: Creating an abstract base class where some methods do nothing, then making subclasses override them — this just moves the LSP violation around.
- **Keeping inheritance and documenting restrictions**: Adding JavaDoc that says "don't call setHeight on Square" is not a fix — code shouldn't rely on documentation to avoid crashes.
- **Over-engineering with interfaces**: Creating an interface with 20 methods when inheritance would work fine — LSP violations only matter when the subclass actually breaks substitution.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Name the exact base guarantee the subtype breaks.
Correct the subtype if it can genuinely honour that guarantee.
Narrow or split an over-broad base contract when capabilities differ.
Use independent types or composition when inheritance is not substitutable.
Run shared contract tests against every implementation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
To fix an LSP violation, first identify the observable base guarantee that fails. The subtype may reject an input the base accepts, weaken its result, break an invariant, or remove a promised operation.

The fix can be to correct the subtype, narrow the base contract, split capabilities into interfaces, or remove the inheritance relationship. For the mutable rectangle and square case, separate immutable `Shape` implementations can expose `area()` without promising independent setters. A caching service can wrap a correct service through composition while preserving its contract.

Removing inheritance is common but not automatic. The final design is correct when every advertised implementation passes the same contract tests and clients no longer need subtype-specific checks or exceptions.

question: When does UnsupportedOperationException indicate an LSP problem?
title: UnsupportedOperationException and LSP violation
direct_answer: UnsupportedOperationException indicates an LSP problem when the parent contract promises that the operation is supported but a subtype rejects it. It is not automatically a violation: Java APIs such as List explicitly document optional operations, so callers must not assume every List is mutable. A clearer capability-specific interface is often better when callers need that guarantee.

sections.title: Why UnsupportedOperationException Violates LSP
sections.content:
`UnsupportedOperationException` is evidence of an LSP problem only after reading the **contract**. If a base type promises that `save` works for every implementation, a `ReadOnlyRepository` that implements that type and rejects `save` cannot safely substitute for it. The subtype has removed a capability its clients were promised.

Java collection interfaces are a useful nuance. The `List` contract documents several modifying methods as **optional operations** and permits them to throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. An unmodifiable list therefore follows the published Java contract, although the broad interface makes mutability easy for a caller to assume incorrectly.

When a capability matters, express it clearly. `CustomerReader` and `CustomerWriter`, or an immutable collection type and a mutable collection type, can communicate more than a runtime exception. The question is not whether an exception appears; it is whether the replacement honors the guarantees its clients are entitled to rely on.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|The Red Flag|~opting out|subclass can't honor a method|throws UnsupportedOperationException
blue|Why It Breaks LSP|~caller surprise|the base promised it works|the subtype refuses at runtime
emerald|Real Example|~immutable List|List.of().add() throws|substitution unsafe
violet|The Fix|~split the interface|MutableList vs ReadOnlyList

sections.title: UnsupportedOperationException LSP Violation
When This Pattern Appears
sections.content:
Treat `UnsupportedOperationException` as a prompt to inspect the contract. It indicates an LSP problem when an implementation rejects an operation that the base type guarantees. If the operation is explicitly optional, as with several Java collection mutators, the exception can follow the published contract.

When callers need a definite capability, prefer a type that states it directly—for example, separate customer reader and writer contracts. This prevents callers from discovering an important limitation only at runtime.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling every UnsupportedOperationException an LSP violation**: first check whether the operation is guaranteed or documented as optional.
- **Hiding a promised capability**: a subtype must not reject behavior its base contract requires.
- **Relying on a broad type when capability matters**: use a focused contract for read-only versus writable behavior.
- **Treating successful compilation as proof of substitutability**: behavior and documented guarantees matter too.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Read the base contract before deciding whether UnsupportedOperationException violates LSP.
It is a violation when a subtype rejects an operation the base contract guarantees.
Java List documents mutating methods as optional, so an unmodifiable List follows that contract.
Optional operations can still produce confusing APIs when callers need a clear capability.
Use focused read/write or mutable/immutable contracts when the distinction matters.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` is not automatically an LSP violation. The decision depends on the contract of the base type. If `CustomerRepository.save` is guaranteed for every repository, a read-only subtype that rejects `save` cannot replace the base type for its clients; it has weakened a promised capability.

Java's `List` is different. Its documentation marks several mutating methods as optional and explicitly allows `UnsupportedOperationException`. An unmodifiable list therefore follows the published `List` contract, even though code that casually assumes all lists are mutable may still fail.

When clients truly require a capability, clearer types are usually safer. A reader can implement `CustomerReader`, while writable implementations also implement `CustomerWriter`. LSP is about honoring observable guarantees, not banning one exception class.

question: How does LSP relate to interface contracts?
title: LSP and interface contracts — behavioral expectations
direct_answer: LSP gives interface and base-class contracts behavioral meaning. An implementation must follow more than the method signature: it must accept valid inputs, provide required results, preserve invariants, and use documented failures. Preconditions cannot be strengthened and postconditions cannot be weakened for a subtype.

sections.title: LSP as Contract Fulfillment
sections.content:
An interface signature describes names and types, but clients also rely on **behavioral guarantees**. These include valid inputs, returned results, state changes, invariants, ordering, idempotency, and documented failure cases.

LSP says an implementation used through that interface must preserve those guarantees. A subtype cannot demand extra conditions that the base did not require, and it cannot deliver less than the base promised. It may accept more inputs or provide a stronger result when that remains compatible.

Contracts should be documented and tested. A shared test suite can run against an in-memory repository and a database repository to verify not-found behavior, duplicate handling, and save semantics. A test double should preserve the behavior relevant to the client rather than return arbitrary values merely to make a test compile.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Contract = Behavior|~not just signatures|pre and postconditions count|exceptions are part of it
blue|Honor the Promise|~implementers|same guarantees as the type|no weaker behavior
emerald|LSP + Interfaces|~design by contract|callers trust the interface|every impl must keep it
violet|Break|~ignored contract|returns null where non-null promised

sections.title: Contract Violation Example
When Contract Thinking Matters
sections.content:
Write behavioral contracts where multiple implementations must be interchangeable: repositories, payment gateways, caches, storage adapters, and test fakes. Document valid inputs, success results, state changes, and expected errors.

Run the same contract tests against each implementation. Do not invent an 'implicit contract' after a failure; make important guarantees explicit enough that implementers and callers can agree on them.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Checking only signatures**: matching parameter and return types does not preserve behavior.
- **Strengthening preconditions**: a subtype cannot reject inputs the base contract accepts.
- **Weakening results or invariants**: an implementation must provide what the contract promises.
- **Assuming one failure style without documentation**: decide whether not-found means empty, null, or an exception and state it.
- **Using a test double with different behavior**: fakes should preserve the guarantees relevant to the client.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: An interface contract includes behavior, not only method signatures.
Subtypes cannot strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions.
Required invariants and documented failures must remain consistent.
Implementations may provide compatible stronger guarantees.
Shared contract tests help verify every implementation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
LSP treats an interface or base class as a behavioral contract. Clients rely not only on parameter and return types, but also on valid inputs, required results, state changes, invariants, and documented errors.

For example, if `CustomerRepository.save` promises to return the persisted customer and reject duplicate email addresses with a documented domain error, both an in-memory test repository and a database repository must preserve those behaviors. Returning `null` from one implementation would break substitutability even though the signature compiles.

Formally, a subtype must not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions, and it must preserve invariants. Shared contract tests are a practical way to check those guarantees across implementations.

question: What is the difference between is-a and behaves-like-a in inheritance?
title: is-a vs behaves-like-a — LSP in inheritance design
direct_answer: An is-a statement describes a category, but inheritance also creates a behavioral contract. A subtype is safe only when it behaves as clients of the base type expect: it accepts valid inputs, preserves required results and invariants, and does not remove promised capabilities. A real-world category alone is not enough to justify extends.

sections.title: Structural vs Behavioral Relationships
sections.content:
An **is-a** statement is about classification: a square is a rectangle in geometry, and a penguin is a bird in biology. Java inheritance means more than classification because a subtype can be passed to code written for its base type. That code relies on behavior.

A subtype therefore has to **behave like** the base contract. It must not demand stronger preconditions, return weaker results, break invariants, or remove capabilities that clients were promised. The classic mutable rectangle/square model fails when the rectangle contract allows width and height to change independently. The problem comes from the setters' behavior, not from geometry.

Model capabilities explicitly. Immutable `Shape` implementations can each provide `area()`. Birds that fly can implement `Flyable`, while penguins need not. Composition may help when one object uses another object's service, but a penguin should not 'contain a bird' merely to avoid inheritance; the types should reflect the behavior the program uses.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|IS-A|~structural|Square is-a Rectangle (math)|name and shape match only
blue|BEHAVES-LIKE-A|~behavioral|must act like the base everywhere|the real LSP test
emerald|Why It Matters|~is-a can lie|Penguin is-a Bird but can't fly()
violet|Rule|~inherit on behavior|if behaves-like-a fails → compose

rows: Is it enough for Java inheritance?
Yes, when the full base contract is preserved
A square is a rectangle in geometry
Mutable independent setters may make substitution unsafe
Flying should be a separate capability if not every bird can fly
Do valid inputs, results, invariants, and capabilities remain compatible?

sections.title: When to Apply Each Concept
sections.content:
Use **is-a thinking** for domain modeling and documentation — understanding that a SavingsAccount is-a BankAccount helps you organize concepts and name classes clearly. But use **behaves-like-a thinking** for actual inheritance decisions. Before making class B extend class A, ask: "Can B be used everywhere A is used without surprises?" In Spring Boot **entity modeling**, an Employee might is-a Person taxonomically, but if Employee has required fields like employeeId and department that Person doesn't, and code operates on Person objects assuming those fields are absent, inheritance breaks.

Use **composition instead** — Employee has-a Person. For **service classes**, if you're creating specialized services, check behavioral compatibility: does CachedOrderService truly behave like OrderService in every scenario, or does it skip database writes? If it skips, don't inherit.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Modeling the real world directly**: Freshers learn domain concepts like "a car is a vehicle" and immediately create class Car extends Vehicle, without checking if the code actually needs that relationship or if behavioral contracts match.
- **Inheritance for code reuse**: Using inheritance just to reuse methods — "User has a login method, so AdminUser should extend User to get it" — even when admin login behavior is different, violating LSP.
- **Biology and math as OOP rules**: Thinking "a penguin is a bird, and birds fly, so penguin should inherit fly method" — then overriding fly to do nothing or throw an exception, which is an LSP violation.
- **Ignoring invariants**: Employee is-a Person, so extending Person seems right, but if Person has an invariant that SSN is optional and Employee requires it, the invariant is broken.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Is-a describes a category; inheritance also promises substitutable behavior.
A subtype must preserve the base type's observable contract.
Real-world taxonomy does not automatically justify a Java extends relationship.
The mutable rectangle/square problem comes from incompatible setter guarantees.
Model capabilities such as `Flyable` or use independent implementations when behavior differs.

sections.title: Code Example
Interview answer
sections.content:
An is-a relationship describes classification, while behaves-like-a describes the contract needed for safe substitution. Java inheritance should satisfy both only when code using the base type can receive the subtype without losing promised behavior.

The usual rectangle and square example depends on a mutable rectangle contract. If callers may set width and height independently, a square subtype cannot preserve that behavior because changing one side must change the other. Both shapes can instead implement an immutable `Shape` contract with `area()`. In the same way, a penguin can be a `Bird` without implementing a separate `Flyable` capability.

The design test is observable behavior: valid base inputs remain valid, required results and invariants remain true, and promised operations remain available. Domain vocabulary starts the model, but the client contract decides whether inheritance is safe.
